analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to annually disclose sexual harassment and abuse settlement totals, including executive misconduct.
analysis.headline: Introduced with eight senators' support, the bill sat in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend securities law so that companies required to file annual Form 10-K reports must tell shareholders and the public how many sexual abuse, harassment, and discrimination settlements and judgments they paid, the dollar totals, how many involve corporate executives, and how long complaints take to resolve. It bars companies and the Securities and Exchange Commission from naming victims, and lets a victim block reporting of a specific settlement. Companies would also have to describe what they do to prevent such misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of publicly traded companies and their contractors and subsidiaries, who would gain a public record of how often their employers pay to settle sexual abuse, harassment, and discrimination claims — including claims against executives — creating pressure from investors, journalists, and job seekers to fix problems. Investors and the public would also see numbers that are currently hidden by confidential settlements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and job seekers at public companies

how_it_helps.text: Each Form 10-K filer must disclose annually the number of settlements and judgments tied to alleged sexual abuse, harassment, or discrimination, the total dollars paid, and the date of each alleged act [S2][S3].
Disclosures must separately count settlements and judgments tied to corporate executives, exposing how often top leadership is involved [S2][S3].
Companies must report pending complaints in internal, arbitration, and litigation channels, plus the average time to resolve them, and describe their prevention measures [S3].
Victims are protected: companies and the SEC may never disclose a victim's name, and a victim can object to having a specific settlement counted, though the count must appear in later years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies bear the cost of collecting and reporting this data every year, and executives face public, individually attributed tallies of misconduct settlements that could affect their careers, compensation, and the company's reputation with investors and recruits.

drawbacks.text: The disclosures count allegations, not proven wrongdoing; a company could look bad from settlements it paid to avoid litigation costs even where claims were weak, and the requirement covers only public companies while private employers stay off the books [S3].

Collecting and categorizing settlement and complaint data — including 7-year historical totals and per-case detail — is a real compliance burden, especially for large companies with many subsidiaries and contractors in scope [S3].

Public tallies may make some companies more resistant to settling at all, or to keeping complainants employed during an internal process, since every dollar and case would become visible to investors and reporters [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is real but indirect: no private right of action or new legal claim is created — the bill's leverage is transparency, relying on investors and public opinion to pressure companies. The main costs are compliance work and the possibility that unproven allegations become public reputational numbers, softened by the victim's right to object and the ban on naming victims. On balance a modest, low-cost transparency rule whose benefit depends on markets and media actually acting on the numbers.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced the bill and it went to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the two-year Congress [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 1, 2023 with seven cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies and their executives avoided a mandatory public tally of sexual misconduct settlements and judgments; workers and investors lost the disclosure they would have gained.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven cosponsors.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred; it died there without action.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's allied independent, no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever held, so the record shows only one-sided Democratic support [S4].

industries.note: Form 10-K filers would have to publicly report counts and dollar totals of sexual abuse, harassment, and discrimination settlements, judgments, and open complaints each year, including through subsidiaries and contractors. That ends the confidentiality companies currently get from settlement agreements and creates reputational and investor pressure they avoid today [S3].

Executives' misconduct settlements and judgments must be counted and priced separately from ordinary employees' cases, attaching personally attributable numbers to leadership. Executives are the category the bill singles out, and its death leaves their settlement records private [S3].
